messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 42
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: South Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Maid
- Trauma Type: Stalking
- Pcl5: 64

Priya is 42 years old. She lives with her husband in a small apartment on the third floor of a aging building in a crowded suburb. Every morning by six she is already on the bus, her cleaning supplies in a worn tote bag, heading to the houses she cleans for cash. She has been a maid for fifteen years. She is good at it—thorough, quiet, invisible. That invisibility is what she used to rely on.

It started two years ago. A man began waiting for her outside one of the houses she cleaned regularly. At first she thought nothing of it. He was always there when she left, sometimes leaning against a wall, sometimes sitting in a car. He would smile. She would nod and walk faster. Then he started leaving things: a folded note under her bag, a small flower on the doorstep. The notes said *You are beautiful when you work* and *I watch you every day*. She tore them up and threw them away. She did not tell her husband. He would have said she was imagining things, or that she had done something to encourage the man.

The stalking escalated. He began following her bus. She would see him two seats back, pretending to read a newspaper. He once stood outside her apartment building for three hours. She watched him from behind the curtain, her heart pounding so hard she felt it in her throat. She called the police. They told her to stay inside at night and call if he touched her.

Now, in the present, Priya’s life has shrunk. She no longer takes the same route to work. She changes buses three times, even though it makes her late. She avoids the house where the stalking began, and lost that regular income. Her current clients notice she is jumpy. She flinches when someone taps her on the shoulder. She cleans with the curtains drawn, and she checks the locks on every door and window twice before she starts scrubbing. Her hands tremble when she sees a man in a similar jacket. She has stopped going to the market alone. Her husband complains that she is distant, that she wakes him with her nightmares. She does not tell him what she sees in the dark: the man’s face, his smile, the way he knew her schedule better than she did.

At the houses she still cleans, Priya is always listening. She hears footsteps on the stairs and freezes, clutching her rag. She cannot concentrate. She replays the notes in her head, the way he wrote her name. She thinks she sees him in the reflection of a window. She avoids leaving her apartment on weekends. She has stopped calling her sister in Mumbai because she cannot explain why she feels so scared all the time.

Her body is always tense. She has headaches that start behind her eyes and do not go away. She feels as though someone is watching her from every parked car, every bus stop. She cannot remember the last time she felt safe. She does not leave her cell phone on silent. She holds it in her pocket while she cleans, ready to dial 911 if she hears his voice. But he has not come near her in eight months. That is the worst part. She does not know why he stopped. She does not know if he will start again. The not knowing is a weight on her chest, a constant vigilance that never lets her rest.
